claim: hTMEM266 is a protein of unknown function that is predicted to contain an S1-S4 domain, along with partially structured cytoplasmic termini.
source: hTMEM266 is a protein of unknown function that is predicted to contain an S1-S4 domain, along with partially structured cytoplasmic termini.
evidence: This statement is directly made in the abstract and is supported by the bioinformatic analysis and homology modeling presented in the manuscript.

claim: hTMEM266 forms oligomers.
source: Here we show that hTMEM266 forms oligomers, undergoes both rapid (µs) and slow (ms) structural rearrangements in response to changes in voltage, and contains a Zn2+ binding site that can regulate the slow conformational transition.
evidence: This claim is supported by biochemical experiments including DSS crosslinking, disulfide-mediated dimerization, and co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: hTMEM266 undergoes rapid (µs) structural rearrangements in response to changes in voltage.
source: Here we show that hTMEM266 forms oligomers, undergoes both rapid (µs) and slow (ms) structural rearrangements in response to changes in voltage, and contains a Zn2+ binding site that can regulate the slow conformational transition.
evidence: This is supported by voltage-clamp fluorimetry experiments showing fluorescence changes with time constants as fast as 130 µs (Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).

claim: hTMEM266 undergoes slow (ms) structural rearrangements in response to changes in voltage.
source: Here we show that hTMEM266 forms oligomers, undergoes both rapid (µs) and slow (ms) structural rearrangements in response to changes in voltage, and contains a Zn2+ binding site that can regulate the slow conformational transition.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the slow fluorescence quenching component observed for P194C labeled with TAMRA-MTS (Figure 5) and the hTMEM266-EGFP construct (Figure 8).

claim: hTMEM266 contains a Zn2+ binding site that can regulate the slow conformational transition.
source: Here we show that hTMEM266 forms oligomers, undergoes both rapid (µs) and slow (ms) structural rearrangements in response to changes in voltage, and contains a Zn2+ binding site that can regulate the slow conformational transition.
evidence: This is supported by experiments showing that extracellular Zn2+ modulates fluorescence signals, particularly the slow component, with low micromolar affinity (Figures 6, 7, 8).

claim: The S1-S4 domain in hTMEM266 is a functional voltage sensor.
source: Our results demonstrate that the S1-S4 domain in hTMEM266 is a functional voltage sensor, motivating future studies to identify cellular processes that may be regulated by the protein.
evidence: This conclusion is based on multiple lines of evidence including chimera experiments (Figure 2), voltage-clamp fluorimetry (Figures 3-5), and quencher accessibility experiments (Figure 4).

claim: The ability of hTMEM266 to respond to voltage on the µs timescale may be advantageous for designing new genetically encoded voltage indicators.
source: The ability of hTMEM266 to respond to voltage on the µs timescale may be advantageous for designing new genetically encoded voltage indicators.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the rapid kinetics observed in the fluorescence experiments.

claim: Voltage-activated K+ (Kv), Na+ (Nav) and Ca2+ (Cav) channels contain S1-S4 domains capable of sensing changes in membrane voltage and triggering opening or closing of a coupled ion selective pore.
source: The voltage-activated K+ (Kv), Na+ (Nav) and Ca2+ (Cav) channels that are required for these forms of electrical signaling all contain S1-S4 domains capable of sensing changes in membrane voltage and triggering opening or closing of a coupled ion selective pore (Swartz, 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by citation to Swartz, 2008.

claim: Movements of the Arg-rich S4 helices drive voltage-sensor activation.
source: it has been established that movements of the Arg-rich S4 helices drive voltage-sensor activation (Bezanilla, 2008; Swartz, 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Bezanilla, 2008 and Swartz, 2008.

claim: S1-S4 voltage-sensing domains have been identified in voltage-sensitive phosphatases (VSPs), where membrane voltage can regulate the catalytic activity of a cytoplasmic lipid phosphatase domain.
source: S1-S4 voltage-sensing domains have also been identified in voltage-sensitive phosphatases (VSPs), where membrane voltage can regulate the catalytic activity of a cytoplasmic lipid phosphatase domain (Grimm and Isacoff, 2016; Kohout et al., 2010; Kohout et al., 2008; Li et al., 2014; Murata et al., 2005; Okamura et al., 2009; Sakata et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: Voltage-activated proton (Hv1) channels contain an S1-S4 domain that also forms the permeation pathway for protons.
source: Subsequent studies showed that voltage-activated proton (Hv1) channels contain an S1-S4 domain that also forms the permeation pathway for protons (Berger and Isacoff, 2011; Lee et al., 2009; Mony et al., 2015; Ramsey et al., 2006; Sasaki et al., 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: hTMEM266 was previously reported to not form functional voltage-activated proton channels.
source: Although the sequence of the S1-S4 domain of hTMEM266 is similar to Hv1, it was previously reported to not form functional voltage-activated proton channels (Kim et al., 2014; Musset et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kim et al., 2014 and Musset et al., 2011.

claim: The S4 helix of hTMEM266 can support voltage-dependent opening when transplanted into Hv1.
source: We demonstrate that its S4 helix can support voltage-dependent opening when transplanted into either Hv1 or Shaker Kv channels.
evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiological recordings of the Hv1-hTMEM266 chimera shown in Figure 2E,F.

claim: The S4 helix of hTMEM266 can support voltage-dependent opening when transplanted into Shaker Kv channels.
source: We demonstrate that its S4 helix can support voltage-dependent opening when transplanted into either Hv1 or Shaker Kv channels.
evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiological recordings of the Shaker-hTMEM266 chimera shown in Figure 2G,H.

claim: Extracellular Zn2+ ions regulate the conformational dynamics of hTMEM266.
source: we show that extracellular Zn2+ ions regulate these conformational dynamics.
evidence: This is demonstrated by voltage-clamp fluorimetry experiments showing that Zn2+ modulates both rapid and slow fluorescence components (Figures 6, 7, 8).

claim: hTMEM266 contains a functional voltage sensor with properties that distinguish it from conventional S1-S4 voltage-sensing domains.
source: We conclude that hTMEM266 contains a functional voltage sensor with properties that distinguish it from conventional S1-S4 voltage-sensing domains.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the unique kinetic properties and voltage-dependence observed in the fluorescence experiments.

claim: The hTMEM266 protein can be identified in BLAST searches using the Hv1 channel as a query.
source: The hTMEM266 protein can be identified in BLAST searches using the Hv1 channel as a query (Kim et al., 2014; Musset et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kim et al., 2014 and Musset et al., 2011.

claim: The hTMEM266 sequence is 531 amino acids long.
source: The hTMEM266 sequence is 531 amino acids long and is predicted to contain four transmembrane (TM) helices that are flanked by an N-terminus containing approximately 100 residues and a C-terminus containing about 310 residues.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the protein sequence.

claim: hTMEM266 is predicted to contain four transmembrane (TM) helices that are flanked by an N-terminus containing approximately 100 residues and a C-terminus containing about 310 residues.
source: The hTMEM266 sequence is 531 amino acids long and is predicted to contain four transmembrane (TM) helices that are flanked by an N-terminus containing approximately 100 residues and a C-terminus containing about 310 residues.
evidence: This is based on bioinformatic predictions and homology modeling.

claim: The four TMs of hTMEM266 are clearly related to the S1-S4 voltage-sensing domains found in Hv1, VSPs and voltage-activated cation channels.
source: The four TMs are clearly related to the S1-S4 voltage-sensing domains found in Hv1, VSPs and voltage-activated cation channels (Figure 1A and see below).
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Among proteins that contain S1-S4 voltage-sensing domains, TMEM266 has the most restricted distribution among species, with orthologous sequences restricted to the genomes of vertebrates.
source: Among proteins that contain S1-S4 voltage-sensing domains, TMEM266 has the most restricted distribution among species, with orthologous sequences restricted to the genomes of vertebrates (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The sequences of TMEM266 orthologs are well conserved, with greater than 50% identity among the most distant branches of the tree and over 80% sequence identity within the S1-S4 domain.
source: The sequences of TMEM266 orthologs are well conserved, with greater than 50% identity among the most distant branches of the tree and over 80% sequence identity within the S1-S4 domain (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Hv1 is the closest relative of hTMEM266 among proteins with S1-S4 domains.
source: The sole region where there is homology with other proteins is the S1-S4 domain, where Hv1 is the closest relative.
evidence: This is inferred from sequence homology searches and alignments.

claim: The N-terminus of hTMEM266 is predicted to contain two short helices that may form a compact domain.
source: Secondary structure predictions suggest that the N-terminus of hTMEM266 contains two short helices that may form a compact domain and that the initial part of the C-terminus forms a helical extension of the S4 helix that is likely to form a coiled-coil (Figure 1B), similar to the C-terminal coiled-coil domain of Hv1 that serves to assemble Hv1 into dimers (Koch et al., 2008; Lee et al., 2008; Qiu et al., 2013; Tombola et al., 2008; Tombola et al., 2010).
evidence: This is based on secondary structure predictions and homology modeling shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The initial part of the C-terminus of hTMEM266 forms a helical extension of the S4 helix that is likely to form a coiled-coil.
source: Secondary structure predictions suggest that the N-terminus of hTMEM266 contains two short helices that may form a compact domain and that the initial part of the C-terminus forms a helical extension of the S4 helix that is likely to form a coiled-coil (Figure 1B), similar to the C-terminal coiled-coil domain of Hv1 that serves to assemble Hv1 into dimers (Koch et al., 2008; Lee et al., 2008; Qiu et al., 2013; Tombola et al., 2008; Tombola et al., 2010).
evidence: This is based on secondary structure predictions and homology modeling shown in Figure 1B, and is supported by biochemical data showing dimerization.

claim: The C-terminal coiled-coil domain of Hv1 serves to assemble Hv1 into dimers.
source: Secondary structure predictions suggest that the N-terminus of hTMEM266 contains two short helices that may form a compact domain and that the initial part of the C-terminus forms a helical extension of the S4 helix that is likely to form a coiled-coil (Figure 1B), similar to the C-terminal coiled-coil domain of Hv1 that serves to assemble Hv1 into dimers (Koch et al., 2008; Lee et al., 2008; Qiu et al., 2013; Tombola et al., 2008; Tombola et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: hTMEM266 family members have ~250 additional residues following the coiled-coil that is predicted to be structurally disordered.
source: Whereas the Hv1 sequence terminates at the coiled-coil, hTMEM266 family members have ~250 additional residues following the coiled-coil that is predicted by multiple secondary structure prediction programs to be structurally disordered (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is based on secondary structure predictions shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The S4 helix of hTMEM266 contains three Arg residues (R208, R211 and R214) positioned according to the RXXRXXR motif common to the S4 helix of all voltage-sensing domains.
source: Like Hv1, the S4 helix of hTMEM266 contains three Arg residues (R208, R211 and R214) positioned according to the RXXRXXR motif common to the S4 helix of all voltage-sensing domains, where X is typically a hydrophobic residue.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The S1-S4 domain of hTMEM266 contains a triad of residues (F149 and E152 in the S2 helix, as well as D174 in the S3 helix) that in other S1-S4 domains has been termed the 'charge-transfer center'.
source: The S1-S4 domain of hTMEM266 also has a triad of residues (F149 and E152 in the S2 helix, as well as D174 in the S3 helix) that in other S1-S4 domains has been termed the 'charge-transfer center' because they facilitate movement of the positively charged residues in S4 across the membrane (Tao et al., 2010).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis and comparison with other voltage-sensing domains, supported by citation to Tao et al., 2010.

claim: In the homology model of hTMEM266, all three Arg residues on the S4 helix face in towards the domain core with the middle Arg positioned closest to F149 within the charge transfer center.
source: In the homology model, all three Arg residues on the S4 helix face in towards the domain core with the middle Arg positioned closest to F149 within the charge transfer center, leaving the first Arg external to F149, and the third Arg internal to F149 (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is based on the homology model shown in Figure 1C.

claim: hTMEM266 contains acidic and/or polar residues positioned above (E118 on the S1 helix and S142 on the S2 helix) and below (E152 on the S2 helix and both E171 and D174 on the S3 helix) the charge transfer center that could potentially stabilize the positively charged S4 Arg residues within the membrane.
source: Like other S1-S4 domains, hTMEM266 also contains acidic and/or polar residues positioned above (E118 on the S1 helix and S142 on the S2 helix) and below (E152 on the S2 helix and both E171 and D174 on the S3 helix) the charge transfer center that could potentially stabilize the positively charged S4 Arg residues within the membrane (Long et al., 2007; Papazian et al., 1995).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis and comparison with other voltage-sensing domains, supported by citations.

claim: hTMEM266 appears to share a Zn2+ binding site with Hv1.
source: Finally, hTMEM266 appears to share a Zn2+ binding site with Hv1.
evidence: This is based on sequence conservation and functional experiments with Zn2+.

claim: In Hv1, four residues (E115 and D119 in S1, H136 in S2 and H189 in S4) have been implicated in coordinating Zn2+.
source: In Hv1, four residues (E115 and D119 in S1, H136 in S2 and H189 in S4; numbering for mHv1) have been implicated in coordinating Zn2+, a metal ion that inhibits the proton channel by stabilizing a closed state of the channel (Ramsey et al., 2006; Takeshita et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Ramsey et al., 2006 and Takeshita et al., 2014.

claim: Three of the four Zn2+-coordinating residues in Hv1 are conserved in hTMEM266 (E118 and D122 in S1 and H139 in S2).
source: Three of these four Zn2+-coordinating residues are conserved in hTMEM266 (E118 and D122 in S1 and H139 in S2), while a Ser (S196 in S4) is present at the equivalent position of H189 in Hv1 (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment shown in Figure 1A.

claim: hTMEM266 contains an additional Lys residue (K213) just before the third Arg residue in the S4 helix.
source: Although the 'X' amino acids in the RXXRXXR motif in the S4 helix are generally non-polar, hTMEM266 contains an additional Lys residue (K213) just before the third Arg residue (Figure 1A,C).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis shown in Figure 1A,C.

claim: In the homology model of hTMEM266, K213 projects out from the domain, raising the possibility that it may be involved in oligomerization.
source: In our homology model, K213 projects out from the domain (Figure 1C), raising the possibility that it may be involved in oligomerization (see below).
evidence: This is a speculation based on the homology model shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The S4 helix of hTMEM266 contains an acidic residue (D217) following and in register with the S4 Arg residues.
source: The S4 helix of hTMEM266 also contains an acidic residue (D217) following and in register with the S4 Arg residues, a feature also seen in the S4 helices of EAG and ERG Kv channels (Wang and MacKinnon, 2017; Whicher and MacKinnon, 2016), but that is otherwise uncommon in voltage-sensing domains.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis and comparison with other voltage-sensing domains, supported by citations.

claim: hTMEM266 has non-polar residues (V111 in S1 and M185 in S3) in the core of the 4TM bundle that are typically charged or polar in other voltage-sensing domains.
source: Finally, hTMEM266 has non-polar residues (V111 in S1 and M185 in S3) in the core of the 4TM bundle that are typically charged or polar in other voltage-sensing domains, leading to a larger cluster of hydrophobic residues external to the charge transfer center (Figure 1A,C).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis and homology modeling shown in Figure 1A,C.

claim: hTMEM266 does not form functional proton channels when expressed in HEK cells.
source: We began by confirming that hTMEM266 does not form functional proton channels when expressed in HEK cells and studied using whole-cell patch clamp recordings with solutions optimized for recording proton currents.
evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 2A,B.

claim: A C-terminally GFP-tagged construct of hTMEM266 traffics efficiently to the plasma membrane.
source: even though a C-terminally GFP-tagged construct of hTMEM266 traffics efficiently to the plasma membrane (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by confocal microscopy shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: When hHv1 and hTMEM266 were expressed together, voltage-activated proton currents were indistinguishable from Hv1 alone.
source: However, when hHv1 and hTMEM266 were expressed together, we measured voltage-activated proton currents that were indistinguishable from Hv1 alone (Figure 2A–C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 2A–C.

claim: hTMEM266 does not alter the functional properties of Hv1 when the two proteins are co-expressed.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that hTMEM266 is not a proton channel and does not alter the functional properties of Hv1 when the two proteins are co-expressed.
evidence: This conclusion is based on electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 2A–C.

claim: Transfer of the S4 helix from hTMEM266 into hHv1 results in functional voltage-activated proton channels.
source: Transfer of the S4 helix from hTMEM266 into hHv1 results in functional voltage-activated proton channels when expressed in HEK cells, with a voltage-activation relation that is shifted to more depolarized voltages compared to Hv1 (Figure 2E,F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 2E,F.

claim: The hHv1-hTMEM266 chimera has a voltage-activation relation that is shifted to more depolarized voltages compared to Hv1.
source: Transfer of the S4 helix from hTMEM266 into hHv1 results in functional voltage-activated proton channels when expressed in HEK cells, with a voltage-activation relation that is shifted to more depolarized voltages compared to Hv1 (Figure 2E,F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 2E,F.

claim: Transplantation of the S3b-S4 paddle motif from hTMEM266 into the Shaker Kv channel results in a functional chimera.
source: We also succeeded in generating a functional chimera wherein the S3b-S4 paddle motif was transplanted from hTMEM266 into the Shaker Kv channel, and when expressed in oocytes this chimera also displayed a similarly shifted voltage-activation relation (Figure 2G,H).
evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 2G,H.

claim: The Shaker-hTMEM266 chimera displays a shifted voltage-activation relation compared to Shaker.
source: We also succeeded in generating a functional chimera wherein the S3b-S4 paddle motif was transplanted from hTMEM266 into the Shaker Kv channel, and when expressed in oocytes this chimera also displayed a similarly shifted voltage-activation relation (Figure 2G,H).
evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 2G,H.

claim: The S4 helix of hTMEM266 can support voltage-dependent gating in the context of two distinct voltage-activated ion channels.
source: These perturbations in the energetics of voltage-dependent gating are relatively modest when considering how many residues differ between the transferred regions of hTMEM266 and either hHv1 or Shaker (Figure 2D) and indicate that the S4 helix of hTMEM266 can support voltage-dependent gating in the context of two distinct voltage-activated ion channels.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the functional chimera experiments shown in Figure 2.

claim: The Hv1 channel forms dimers and the C-terminal coiled-coil extension of the S4 helix mediates dimerization.
source: Functional and biochemical experiments have established that the Hv1 channel forms dimers and that the C-terminal coiled-coil extension of the S4 helix mediates dimerization (Gonzalez et al., 2010; Koch et al., 2008; Lee et al., 2008; Tombola et al., 2008; Tombola et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: Exposure of cells expressing hTMEM266 to disuccinimidyl substerate (DSS) resulted in formation of a higher molecular weight band in Western blots, consistent with dimer formation.
source: Exposure of cells expressing hTMEM266 to disuccinimidyl substerate (DSS), a bifunctional membrane permeable primary amine crosslinking reagent, resulted in formation of a higher molecular weight band in Western blots of PAGE gels (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,C), consistent with dimer formation.
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,C.

claim: The C-terminal coiled-coil of hTMEM266 contains a Cys residue (C252) that is conserved in Hv1 where it can form a disulfide bond in the coiled-coil.
source: Because the C-terminal coiled-coil of hTMEM266 contains a Cys residue (C252) that is conserved in Hv1 where it can form a disulfide bond in the coiled-coil (Fujiwara et al., 2013), we expressed the coiled-coil of hTMEM266 alone (residues 224–289) and tested whether the purified domain could form dimers.
evidence: This is based on sequence conservation and citation to Fujiwara et al., 2013.

claim: The purified coiled-coil domain of hTMEM266 can form disulfide-mediated dimers.
source: In contrast, under non-reducing conditions a substantial fraction of the protein migrated at a higher molecular weight (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D), suggesting that the coiled-coil can form disulfide-mediated dimers.
evidence: This is demonstrated by SDS-PAGE analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2D.

claim: Disulfide-mediated dimers of hTMEM266 can form.
source: We also observed the presence of a higher molecular weight band in Western blots of hTMEM266 under non-reducing conditions (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B,C), suggesting that disulfide-mediated dimers of hTMEM266 can form.
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B,C.

claim: The C-terminus of hTMEM266 mediates dimerization.
source: In this context, deletion of the coiled-coil containing C-terminus of hTMEM266 from the GFP-tagged construct prevented pulldown along with the Strep-tagged protein, indicating that the C-terminus of hTMEM266 mediates dimerization.
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2E,F.

claim: The coiled-coil of hTMEM266 can mediate dimerization of the full-length protein.
source: From these results, we conclude that coiled-coil of hTMEM266 can mediate dimerization of the full-length protein.
evidence: This conclusion is based on multiple biochemical experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Eight of the 15 positions between the outer ends of S3 and S4 appeared to be accessible to the extracellular solution as the fluorescence intensity after TAMRA-MTS labelling was greater than for oocytes that expressed WT hTMEM266 or were not injected with cRNA.
source: Eight of the 15 positions appeared to be accessible to the extracellular solution as the fluorescence intensity after TAMRA-MTS labelling was greater than for oocytes that expressed WT hTMEM266 or were not injected with cRNA (uninjected) (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by fluorescence intensity measurements shown in Figure 3A.

claim: For eight positions between the outer ends of S3 and S4, rapid fluorescence increases (dequenching) were observed following membrane depolarization.
source: In addition, whereas the fluorescence from control oocytes (uninjected or WT hTMEM266) did not change appreciably when membrane voltage was stepped between −200 and +200 mV, for these eight positions we observed rapid fluorescence increases (dequenching) following membrane depolarization (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by voltage-clamp fluorimetry shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The size of the fluorescence change (ΔF/F) for TAMRA-labeled hTMEM266 constructs ranged from 1% to 5%.
source: The size of the fluorescence change (ΔF/F) ranged from 1% to 5% (Figure 3B,C) with nearly linear F-V relations that did not saturate over a voltage range of −200 to +200 mV (Figure 3C,D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by voltage-clamp fluorimetry shown in Figure 3B,C.

claim: TAMRA-labeled hTMEM266 constructs showed nearly linear F-V relations that did not saturate over a voltage range of −200 to +200 mV.
source: The size of the fluorescence change (ΔF/F) ranged from 1% to 5% (Figure 3B,C) with nearly linear F-V relations that did not saturate over a voltage range of −200 to +200 mV (Figure 3C,D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by voltage-clamp fluorimetry shown in Figure 3C,D.

claim: For hTMEM266 P194C, a rapid increase in fluorescence with depolarization was followed by a slower decrease (quenching).
source: Two of the positions also showed a second, slower phase in the fluorescence signals; for hTMEM266 P194C, we typically observed a rapid increase in fluorescence with depolarization, followed by a slower decrease (quenching), and for hTMEM266 W198C, we observed both rapid and slow phases of dequenching (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by voltage-clamp fluorimetry shown in Figure 3C.

claim: For hTMEM266 W198C, both rapid and slow phases of dequenching were observed.
source: Two of the positions also showed a second, slower phase in the fluorescence signals; for hTMEM266 P194C, we typically observed a rapid increase in fluorescence with depolarization, followed by a slower decrease (quenching), and for hTMEM266 W198C, we observed both rapid and slow phases of dequenching (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by voltage-clamp fluorimetry shown in Figure 3C.

claim: For hTMEM266 G193C, the time constant of the fast fluorescence component (τF) was 408 µs in two-electrode voltage clamp mode.
source: For hTMEM266 G193C, a position that lacks the slow quenching component, τF was 408 µs in two-electrode voltage clamp mode, which is close to the value of the clamp speed estimated from the capacitive transient (τQ=571 µs) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by voltage-clamp fluorimetry shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E.

claim: In the cut-open voltage clamp mode, the time constant of the fast fluorescence component (τF) for hTMEM266 G193C was 130 µs.
source: In the faster cut-open voltage clamp mode, we measured a τF of 130 µs for the G193 position when τV was 39 µs.
evidence: This is demonstrated by voltage-clamp fluorimetry in cut-open mode.

claim: The kinetics of the dequenching components for the labeled positions studied are remarkably rapid and are likely limited by the speed of the voltage clamp.
source: Taken together, these observations lead us to conclude that the kinetics of the dequenching components for the labeled positions we studied are remarkably rapid and are likely limited by the speed of our voltage clamp.
evidence: This conclusion is based on comparison of fluorescence kinetics with clamp speed measurements.

claim: The amount of charge measured by integrating transient capacitive currents was larger in oocytes expressing hTMEM266 G193C compared to control un-injected oocytes.
source: Although we could not unambiguously detect non-linear charge movement similar to what has been measured for voltage-sensor activation in voltage-activated ion channels (Bezanilla, 2018) or VSPs (Murata et al., 2005), the amount of charge measured by integrating transient capacitive currents was larger in oocytes expressing hTMEM266 G193C compared to control un-injected oocytes (Figure 3; Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by charge measurements shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Expression of hTMEM266 either contains mobile charges or changes the properties of the plasma membrane.
source: This apparent increase in membrane capacitance suggests either that hTMEM266 contains mobile charges, or that expression of hTMEM266 changes the properties of the plasma membrane, such as its area, thickness or polarizability.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observed increase in apparent capacitance.

claim: The rapid kinetics and near linear F-V relationships observed for most sites in hTMEM266 are quite distinct from TAMRA-MTS labeled Cys mutants of the Shaker Kv channel, Ci-VSP and Hv1.
source: The rapid kinetics and near linear F-V relationships observed for most sites in hTMEM266 are quite distinct from TAMRA-MTS labeled Cys mutants of the Shaker Kv channel, Ci-VSP and Hv1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–C), and raises the possibility that the fluorophore in our hTMEM266 labeled constructs is positioned within the membrane electric field, which might directly alter fluorescence by perturbing the ground or excited energy states of the fluorophore, a mechanism that has been termed the Stark-shift or electrochromic effect (Asamoah et al., 2003; Klymchenko and Demchenko, 2002; Klymchenko et al., 2006).
evidence: This is based on comparison with control experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–C and citations to literature on electrochromic effects.

claim: Anionic I- and zwitterionic tryptophan (Trp) were effective quenchers of TAMRA-MTS in solution at low mM concentrations.
source: We first tested a variety of candidate ions and molecules for quenching of TAMRA-MTS in solution and found that anionic I- and zwitterionic tryptophan (Trp) were effective quenchers at low mM concentrations, and that Ni2+ was effective at higher concentrations (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by solution quenching experiments shown in Figure 4A,B.

claim: Ni2+ was an effective quencher of TAMRA-MTS in solution at higher concentrations.
source: We first tested a variety of candidate ions and molecules for quenching of TAMRA-MTS in solution and found that anionic I- and zwitterionic tryptophan (Trp) were effective quenchers at low mM concentrations, and that Ni2+ was effective at higher concentrations (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by solution quenching experiments shown in Figure 4A,B.

claim: In control experiments with TAMRA-MTS labeling of uninjected oocytes, fluorescence quenching from extracellular Trp or I- was independent of membrane voltage.
source: In control experiments with TAMRA-MTS labeling of uninjected oocytes, fluorescence quenching from extracellular Trp or I- was independent of membrane voltage (Figure 4C; Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by control experiments shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: For cells expressing G193C labeled with TAMRA-MTS, extracellular application of Trp quenched the fluorescence more efficiently when the membrane was depolarized.
source: In contrast, for cells expressing G193C labeled with TAMRA-MTS, extracellular application of Trp quenched the fluorescence more efficiently when the membrane was depolarized, consistent with the fluorophores becoming more accessible to the quencher as the membrane voltage was increased (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quenching experiments shown in Figure 4D.

claim: hTMEM266 undergoes a rapid conformational change with membrane depolarization.
source: Collectively, these experiments with collisional quenchers strongly suggest that hTMEM266 undergoes a rapid conformational change with membrane depolarization.
evidence: This conclusion is based on voltage-dependent quenching experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: Quenching by the negatively charged I- was more voltage-dependent than quenching by the neutral Trp.
source: However, quenching by the negatively charged I- was more voltage-dependent than quenching by the neutral Trp (compare Figure 4F for Trp with Figure 4—figure supplement 2E for I-), suggesting that the electric potential near the fluorophore differs from the bulk solution.
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparison of quenching experiments shown in Figure 4F and Figure 4—figure supplement 2E.

claim: The electric potential near the fluorophore in hTMEM266 differs from the bulk solution.
source: However, quenching by the negatively charged I- was more voltage-dependent than quenching by the neutral Trp (compare Figure 4F for Trp with Figure 4—figure supplement 2E for I-), suggesting that the electric potential near the fluorophore differs from the bulk solution.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential voltage-dependence of quenching by charged vs. neutral quenchers.

claim: For P194C labeled with TAMRA-MTS, the amplitude of the slower component, ΔFslow, can be characterized by the difference between fluorescence levels at the beginning (ΔFi) and end (ΔFe) of the voltage step.
source: As shown in Figure 5A, the amplitude of the slower component, ΔFslow, can be characterized by the difference between fluorescence levels at the beginning (ΔFi) and end (ΔFe) of the voltage step.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 5A.

claim: The amplitude and time constant of the slower fluorescence component in P194C varied between cells.
source: Curiously, the amplitude and time constant of the slower component varied between cells (see Figure 6B–D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the variability shown in Figure 6B–D.

claim: For P194C, the rapid fluorescence component was roughly linear from −200 mV to +200 mV.
source: Whereas the rapid component was roughly linear from −200 mV to +200 mV (Figure 5B), the slow component was essentially undetectable during hyperpolarizing steps, but increased rapidly when the membrane was depolarized without any apparent saturation (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by voltage-clamp fluorimetry shown in Figure 5B.

claim: For P194C, the slow fluorescence component was essentially undetectable during hyperpolarizing steps, but increased rapidly when the membrane was depolarized without any apparent saturation.
source: Whereas the rapid component was roughly linear from −200 mV to +200 mV (Figure 5B), the slow component was essentially undetectable during hyperpolarizing steps, but increased rapidly when the membrane was depolarized without any apparent saturation (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by voltage-clamp fluorimetry shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The slow conformational change in P194C modulated quenching of TAMRA by extracellular Trp and I-.
source: The slower conformational change also modulated quenching of TAMRA attached to P194C by extracellular Trp and I- (Figure 5D–I).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quenching experiments shown in Figure 5D–I.

claim: The slow conformational change reduced the accessibility of the fluorophore to the quencher.
source: Fluorescence quenching rapidly increased at the start of each depolarization step, but then decreased during the step suggesting that the slow conformational change reduced the accessibility of the fluorophore to the quencher (Figure 5D–I).
evidence: This is inferred from the time course of quenching shown in Figure 5D–I.

claim: hTMEM266 undergoes two conformational rearrangements in response to changes in membrane voltage.
source: Collectively, the results presented thus far are consistent with hTMEM266 undergoing two conformational rearrangements in response to changes in membrane voltage.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the observation of both rapid and slow fluorescence components.

claim: The first conformational rearrangement of hTMEM266 occurs rapidly and results in an enhanced accessibility of the fluorophore to collisional quenchers.
source: The first occurs rapidly and results in an enhanced accessibility of the fluorophore to collisional quenchers.
evidence: This is based on the rapid fluorescence changes and voltage-dependent quenching experiments.

claim: The second conformational rearrangement of hTMEM266 occurs on the timescale of milliseconds and reduces TAMRA fluorescence attached at P194C.
source: The second occurs on the timescale of milliseconds and reduces TAMRA fluorescence attached at P194C.
evidence: This is based on the slow fluorescence quenching component observed for P194C.

claim: The slow fluorescence component in P194C is not observed below 0 mV but becomes increasingly apparent as the voltage becomes more depolarized.
source: This second quenching component is not observed below 0 mV but becomes increasingly apparent as the voltage becomes more depolarized.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the voltage-dependence of the slow component shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The Hv1 voltage-activated proton channel is inhibited by micromolar concentrations of Zn2+.
source: The Hv1 voltage-activated proton channel is inhibited by micromolar concentrations of Zn2+ and mutagenesis experiments have implicated two His residues (H136 near S2 and H189 near S4) in forming the Zn2+ binding site (Cherny and DeCoursey, 1999; Musset et al., 2008; Ramsey et al., 2006; Sasaki et al., 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: In Hv1, two His residues (H136 near S2 and H189 near S4) are implicated in forming the Zn2+ binding site.
source: The Hv1 voltage-activated proton channel is inhibited by micromolar concentrations of Zn2+ and mutagenesis experiments have implicated two His residues (H136 near S2 and H189 near S4) in forming the Zn2+ binding site (Cherny and DeCoursey, 1999; Musset et al., 2008; Ramsey et al., 2006; Sasaki et al., 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: The Hv1 crystal structure reveals the likely involvement of two acidic residues (E115 and D119) near the external end of S1 in the Zn2+ binding site.
source: The Hv1 crystal structure is compatible with these His residues contributing to the Zn2+ binding site, but also reveals the likely involvement of two acidic residues (E115 and D119) near the external end of S1 (Takeshita et al., 2014).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis supported by citation to Takeshita et al., 2014.

claim: For P194C labeled with TAMRA-MTS, external Zn2+ ions quenched the rapid fluorescence signals at all voltages.
source: For P194C labeled with TAMRA-MTS, external Zn2+ ions quenched the rapid fluorescence signals at all voltages, inhibited the slow quenching component and steepened the ΔF/F relation (Figure 6).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Zn2+ modulation experiments shown in Figure 6.

claim: For P194C labeled with TAMRA-MTS, external Zn2+ ions inhibited the slow quenching component.
source: For P194C labeled with TAMRA-MTS, external Zn2+ ions quenched the rapid fluorescence signals at all voltages, inhibited the slow quenching component and steepened the ΔF/F relation (Figure 6).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Zn2+ modulation experiments shown in Figure 6.

claim: For P194C labeled with TAMRA-MTS, external Zn2+ ions steepened the ΔF/F relation.
source: For P194C labeled with TAMRA-MTS, external Zn2+ ions quenched the rapid fluorescence signals at all voltages, inhibited the slow quenching component and steepened the ΔF/F relation (Figure 6).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Zn2+ modulation experiments shown in Figure 6.

claim: H139 in S2 is a quenching residue that is largely responsible for the fluorescence signals measured when labeling P194C with TAMRA-MTS.
source: Although these effects of the metal ion are complex, our results show that H139 in S2 is a quenching residue that is largely responsible for the fluorescence signals measured when labeling P194C with TAMRA-MTS, and that H139 also participates in forming the Zn2+ binding site, leading us to conclude that Zn2+ binding modifies the interactions between H139 and TAMRA.
evidence: This is based on mutagenesis experiments shown in Figure 7.

claim: H139 participates in forming the Zn2+ binding site in hTMEM266.
source: Although these effects of the metal ion are complex, our results show that H139 in S2 is a quenching residue that is largely responsible for the fluorescence signals measured when labeling P194C with TAMRA-MTS, and that H139 also participates in forming the Zn2+ binding site, leading us to conclude that Zn2+ binding modifies the interactions between H139 and TAMRA.
evidence: This is based on mutagenesis experiments shown in Figure 7.

claim: Zn2+ binding modifies the interactions between H139 and TAMRA in P194C.
source: Although these effects of the metal ion are complex, our results show that H139 in S2 is a quenching residue that is largely responsible for the fluorescence signals measured when labeling P194C with TAMRA-MTS, and that H139 also participates in forming the Zn2+ binding site, leading us to conclude that Zn2+ binding modifies the interactions between H139 and TAMRA.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the effects of Zn2+ on fluorescence and the role of H139.

claim: Mutation of H139 to Trp altered the slow component of fluorescence change from quenching to dequenching in P194C labeled with TAMRA-MTS.
source: Interestingly, mutation of H139 to Trp, another strong quencher of TAMRA fluorescence, altered the slow component of fluorescence change from quenching to dequenching in P194C labeled with TAMRA-MTS.
evidence: This is demonstrated by mutagenesis experiments shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The H139W mutant alters the position of the quenching residues relative to the fluorophore, effectively altering the state in which quenching is maximal.
source: One explanation for this observation is that the H139W mutant alters the position of the quenching residues relative to the fluorophore, effectively altering the state in which quenching is maximal.
evidence: This is a speculation to explain the observed change in fluorescence behavior.

claim: The effects of Zn2+ on TAMRA-MTS labeled P194C and the hTMEM266-EGFP constructs were clearly distinct.
source: Interestingly, the effects of Zn2+ on TAMRA-MTS labeled P194C and the hTMEM266-EGFP constructs were clearly distinct.
evidence: This is based on comparison of Zn2+ effects shown in Figures 6 and 8.

claim: In hTMEM266-EGFP, Zn2+ augmented the slow quenching component observed at positive membrane voltages and appeared to shift the component to more negative voltages.
source: In hTMEM266-EGFP the metal ion augmented the slow quenching component observed at positive membrane voltages and appeared to shift the component to more negative voltages (Figure 8).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Zn2+ modulation experiments shown in Figure 8.

claim: Zn2+ binding modulates voltage-dependent transitions in hTMEM266.
source: Since Zn2+ binds on the external side of the protein and GFP was inserted into the intracellular C-terminus of the protein, these results indicate that Zn2+ binding modulates voltage-dependent transitions in hTMEM266.
evidence: This is inferred from the effects of Zn2+ on the hTMEM266-EGFP construct.

claim: The Zn2+ binding site in hTMEM266 has low micromolar affinity.
source: To explore the mechanism by which Zn2+ modulates fluorescence signals for TAMRA-MTS labeling of P194C, we first titrated the effects of Zn2+ and found that its binding site in hTMEM266 has low micromolar affinity (Figure 7A,D), somewhat lower affinity than measured in Hv1 (Ramsey et al., 2006), consistent with the fact that hTMEM266 contains three of the four residues implicated in Hv1 (Takeshita et al., 2014).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Zn2+ titration experiments shown in Figure 7A,D.

claim: The Zn2+ binding site in hTMEM266 has somewhat lower affinity than measured in Hv1.
source: To explore the mechanism by which Zn2+ modulates fluorescence signals for TAMRA-MTS labeling of P194C, we first titrated the effects of Zn2+ and found that its binding site in hTMEM266 has low micromolar affinity (Figure 7A,D), somewhat lower affinity than measured in Hv1 (Ramsey et al., 2006), consistent with the fact that hTMEM266 contains three of the four residues implicated in Hv1 (Takeshita et al., 2014).
evidence: This is based on comparison with published data on Hv1, supported by citation to Ramsey et al., 2006.

claim: H139 plays a role in both the rapid dequenching and slow quenching responses observed at P194C.
source: We mutated H139 to Ala in the P194C background and observed only small fluorescence changes with membrane depolarization for TAMRA-MTS labeled cells, consistent with that residue playing a role in both the rapid dequenching and slow quenching responses observed at P194C.
evidence: This is based on mutagenesis experiments shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Extracellular application of Zn2+ at concentrations as high as 1 mM produced only small decreases in fluorescence for the H139A/P194C construct.
source: In addition, extracellular application of Zn2+ at concentrations as high as 1 mM produced only small decreases in fluorescence for that construct, without altering the slope of the ΔF/F relation (Figure 7B,E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Zn2+ modulation experiments shown in Figure 7B,E.

claim: H139 contributes to forming the Zn2+ binding site in hTMEM266.
source: Taken together, these results lead us to conclude that H139 contributes to forming the Zn2+ binding site and to both the fast and slow fluorescence responses observed when P194C is labeled with TAMRA-MTS.
evidence: This conclusion is based on mutagenesis and Zn2+ modulation experiments shown in Figure 7.

claim: Zn2+ binding modulates the interactions between quenching residues and the fluorophore in hTMEM266.
source: The effects of Zn2+ on P194C for both H139A and H139W constructs suggest that Zn2+ binding modulates the interactions between quenching residues and the fluorophore.
evidence: This is inferred from the effects of Zn2+ on different mutant constructs shown in Figure 7.

claim: Expression of hTMEM266-GFP produced only small voltage-dependent fluorescence changes.
source: Although expression of this hTMEM266-GFP construct produced only small voltage-dependent fluorescence changes, they qualitatively resembled those observed for the P194C construct labeled with TAMRA-MTS, showing rapid fluorescence dequenching with membrane depolarization followed by slower fluorescence quenching (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by voltage-clamp fluorimetry shown in Figure 8A.

claim: The fluorescence changes in hTMEM266-EGFP qualitatively resembled those observed for the P194C construct labeled with TAMRA-MTS.
source: Although expression of this hTMEM266-GFP construct produced only small voltage-dependent fluorescence changes, they qualitatively resembled those observed for the P194C construct labeled with TAMRA-MTS, showing rapid fluorescence dequenching with membrane depolarization followed by slower fluorescence quenching (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is based on comparison of fluorescence signals shown in Figures 5 and 8.

claim: The fast dequenching component observed with hTMEM266-EGFP exhibited a nearly linear ΔF/F-V relation.
source: As observed with the external positions labeled with TAMRA-MTS, the fast dequenching component observed with hTMEM266-EGFP exhibited a nearly linear ΔF/F-V relation (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by voltage-clamp fluorimetry shown in Figure 8C.

claim: The slow quenching component in hTMEM266-EGFP was approximately a factor of 10 slower than that seen in TAMRA-MTS labeled P194C construct.
source: The slow quenching component was approximately a factor of 10 slower in the hTMEM266-EGFP construct when compared to that seen in TAMRA-MTS labeled P194C construct, which may be related to the deletion of the C-terminus or the addition of the bulky EGFP protein.
evidence: This is based on comparison of kinetics between the two constructs.

claim: hTMEM266 is most heavily expressed in the central nervous system.
source: hTMEM266 is most heavily expressed in the central nervous system, but it does not appear to function as an ion channel and its biological role has been a mystery (Kim et al., 2014).
evidence: This is based on expression data supported by citation to Kim et al., 2014.

claim: The biological role of hTMEM266 has been a mystery.
source: hTMEM266 is most heavily expressed in the central nervous system, but it does not appear to function as an ion channel and its biological role has been a mystery (Kim et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the manuscript and supported by citation to Kim et al., 2014.

claim: The fluorescence responses observed when introducing Cys residues between the external ends of S3 and S4 and labeling with TAMRA were unusual.
source: The fluorescence responses we observed when introducing Cys residues between the external ends of S3 and S4 and labeling with TAMRA were unusual, requiring extensive characterization to understand the underlying mechanism.
evidence: This is a statement about the nature of the experimental observations.

claim: For G193C where the cut-open configuration was used to optimize the clamp speed, the increase in fluorescence with membrane depolarization occurred with a time constant of 130 µs.
source: in the case of G193C where we used the cut-open configuration to optimize the clamp speed, the increase in fluorescence with membrane depolarization occurred with a time constant of 130 µs.
evidence: This is demonstrated by voltage-clamp fluorimetry in cut-open mode.

claim: The rapid kinetics and nearly linear ΔF/F-V relationships raise the possibility that the fluorescence increases have an electrochromic origin.
source: The rapid kinetics and nearly linear ΔF/F-V relationships raise the possibility that the fluorescence increases have an electrochromic origin (Asamoah et al., 2003; Klymchenko and Demchenko, 2002; Klymchenko et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observed kinetics and voltage-dependence, supported by citations to literature on electrochromic effects.

claim: Only small electrochromic signals have been reported for tetramethylrhodamine maleimide.
source: Furthermore, for most TAMRA-labeled Cys mutants the fraction of fluorescence quenched by Trp, fq, (Figure 4; Figure 4—figure supplement 1) increased following membrane depolarization, consistent with TMEM266 undergoing a voltage-dependent conformational change that increases the accessibility of the fluorophore to neutral quencher molecules in the extracellular solution.
evidence: This is based on citation to Dekel et al., 2012.

claim: In the hTMEM266-EGFP construct the fluorophore (EGFP) resides in the intracellular solution and should not be subject to direct electrochromic effects.
source: Finally, in our TMEM266-EGFP construct in which the fluorophore (EGFP) resides in the intracellular solution (and thus should not be subject to direct electrochromic effects), we again observed rapid changes in fluorescence and a nearly linear ΔF/F-V relations (Figure 8), consistent with TMEM266 undergoing a rapid conformational change in response to membrane voltage.
evidence: This is based on the design of the construct where EGFP is on the intracellular side.

claim: TMEM266 undergoes a slower conformational change that was most evident when labeling P194C with TAMRA-MTS or when studying the hTMEM266-EGFP construct.
source: TMEM266 also appears to undergo a slower conformational change that was most evident when labeling P194C with TAMRA-MTS or when studying our hTMEM266-EGFP construct.
evidence: This is based on the slow fluorescence components observed in Figures 5 and 8.

claim: In both P194C and hTMEM266-EGFP constructs, the slow fluorescence change was only evident for depolarizations above 0 mV but did not appear to saturate even for depolarized voltages as high as +200 mV.
source: In both cases the slow fluorescence change was only evident for depolarizations above 0 mV but did not appear to saturate even for depolarized voltages as high as +200 mV (Figures 4 and 8).
evidence: This is demonstrated by voltage-clamp fluorimetry shown in Figures 5 and 8.

claim: hTMEM266 contains a regulatory Zn2+ binding site on the external side of the S1-S4 domain that is related to the Zn2+ binding site found in Hv1.
source: Our results also demonstrate that hTMEM266 contains a regulatory Zn2+ binding site on the external side of the S1-S4 domain that is related to the Zn2+ binding site found in Hv1.
evidence: This is based on sequence conservation and functional experiments with Zn2+ shown in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: Zn2+ binding modifies the interactions between H139 and TAMRA in P194C.
source: Although these effects of the metal ion are complex, our results show that H139 in S2 is a quenching residue that is largely responsible for the fluorescence signals measured when labeling P194C with TAMRA-MTS, and that H139 also participates in forming the Zn2+ binding site, leading us to conclude that Zn2+ binding modifies the interactions between H139 and TAMRA.
evidence: This conclusion is based on mutagenesis and Zn2+ modulation experiments shown in Figure 7.

claim: The effects of Zn2+ on TAMRA-MTS labeled P194C and the hTMEM266-EGFP constructs indicate that Zn2+ binding modulates voltage-dependent transitions in hTMEM266.
source: Since Zn2+ binds on the external side of the protein and GFP was inserted into the intracellular C-terminus of the protein, these results indicate that Zn2+ binding modulates voltage-dependent transitions in hTMEM266.
evidence: This is inferred from the distinct effects of Zn2+ on the two constructs.

claim: Relatively linear ΔF/F relations have been reported for a variety of genetically encoded voltage indicators engineered from the voltage-sensing domains from voltage-activated ion channels or voltage-sensitive phosphatases.
source: Indeed, relatively linear ΔF/F relations have been reported for a variety of genetically encoded voltage indicators engineered from the voltage-sensing domains from voltage-activated ion channels or voltage-sensitive phosphatases (Abdelfattah et al., 2016; Barnett et al., 2012; Blunck et al., 2004; St-Pierre et al., 2014; Yang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: hTMEM266 contains a functional voltage-sensing domain that is capable of both rapid (µs) and slow (ms) structural rearrangements in response to changes in membrane voltage.
source: Nevertheless, our results collectively demonstrate that hTMEM266 contains a functional voltage-sensing domain that is capable of both rapid (µs) and slow (ms) structural rearrangements in response to changes in membrane voltage.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study based on all the experimental evidence presented.

claim: hTMEM266 has been reported to localize on the post-synaptic side of glutamatergic mossy fibers and granule cells in the cerebellum.
source: hTMEM266 has been reported to localize on the post-synaptic side of glutamatergic mossy fibers and granule cells in the cerebellum (Kim et al., 2014), and having established that hTMEM266 is a functional voltage sensor it will be exciting to explore whether hTMEM266 can specifically interact with intracellular signaling pathways to provide voltage-dependent regulation.
evidence: This is based on localization data supported by citation to Kim et al., 2014.

claim: It will be exciting to explore whether hTMEM266 can specifically interact with intracellular signaling pathways to provide voltage-dependent regulation.

evidence: This is a speculation about future research directions.

claim: The ability of hTMEM266 to respond rapidly to changes in membrane voltage offers the exciting possibility that it may be useful for designing new genetically encodable voltage indicators with particularly rapid responses.

claim: The rapid fluorescence responses observed in hTMEM266 are faster than what has been observed in the voltage sensors used to create the fastest available voltage indicators that are based on fluorescent proteins.
source: Indeed, the rapid fluorescence responses observed here are faster than what has been observed in the voltage sensors used to create the fastest available voltage indicators that are based on fluorescent proteins (Yang and St-Pierre, 2016; Yang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is based on comparison with published data on voltage indicators, supported by citations.
